articles.title: Aditya Dhar says it took 20 years for him to become an overnight sensation with Dhurandhar, credits lady luck Yami Gautam while revealing why they keep their marriage and work distnct: 'This is Saraswati for us'
articles.summary: Filmmaker Aditya Dhar is still getting immense love for the success of 'Dhurandhar' and 'Dhurandhar: The Revenge'.
articles.body: Filmmaker Aditya Dhar is still getting immense love for the success of 'Dhurandhar' and 'Dhurandhar: The Revenge'. The director was recently at an event with wife, actor Yami Gautam where the duo candidly spoke about each other. While Aditya credited Yami for bringing a positive change in his life and helping him narrate India's story to the world, she praised his honesty, integrity, passion and unwavering commitment to filmmaking.Speaking about his journey in cinema, Aditya reflected on the years of hard work that preceded his success, describing it as a long and rewarding journey. He said in at the CNN-News18 Indian of the Year 2026 awards, “I can only say that it took me 20 years to become an overnight sensation. So, it’s been quite a hell of a journey. And the graph has been quite an exciting one. I’m really, really thankful that I’m married to one of the most beautiful human beings I have ever met. My fate changed the moment she entered my life. And I feel that it’s all the lady luck which is helping me tell the Bharat story to the world,” he said.Aditya moved to Mumbai in 2006 to pursue his dream of making films. Over the years, he worked as an assistant director, lyricist and dialogue writer before making his directorial debut with ‘Uri: The Surgical Strike’ in 2019. Starring Vicky Kaushal, the film emerged as a major box-office success and earned Aditya the National Film Award for Best Direction. With ‘Dhurandhar’, he went on to gain wider recognition, making his reflection on his two-decade-long journey all the more significant.Yami, meanwhile, spoke about the qualities that make Aditya stand out both as a filmmaker and as a person. She described him as someone who embodies integrity, honesty, strong character, passion and immense hard work. Reflecting on how the film industry can sometimes leave people bitter or cynical after difficult experiences, she said Aditya has managed to hold on to his kindness and positivity despite the challenges he has faced.She also spoke about his remarkable dedication to his craft, recalling instances when he would spend nearly 70 hours on set without sleeping. According to Yami, his commitment stems from a clear vision and the desire to give everything to a project. She added that bringing such an ambitious vision to life also demands ‘guts’ and the courage to stay true to it.Aditya, in turn, showered Yami with praise, calling her a woman with a “golden heart”. He said he believes audiences have “not seen even 50% of her potential” and lauded her versatility as an actor. He singled out her performances in ‘Article 370’ and ‘Haq’ as some of her finest work, adding that he was excited about her upcoming projects and believed she would deliver exceptional performances in the future.When asked whether directing his wife came with its own challenges, Aditya said they have always kept their professional and personal lives distinct. He explained that even when discussing a possible film, he prefers to follow a formal professional process instead of making an informal offer at home.“Because that actually is kind of the sanctity of our work, because for us, it’s almost like Saraswati. So, it has to be professional when it comes to work,” he said.This is not the first time the couple has spoken about what they admire in each other. In a 2021 interview with Hindustan Times, shortly after their wedding, Yami had opened up about what drew her to Aditya. She said that while sharing similar interests was not necessarily important to her, having the same value system and ethics mattered greatly. She also spoke about the immense respect she has for him, both as a filmmaker and as a person.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: 'I Play Rocky' star Anthony Ippolito packed on weight with 'entire lifestyle shift' to play Sylvester Stallone
articles.summary: Anthony Ippolito gained more than 30 pounds and trained in a boxing gym to transform into Sylvester Stallone's Rocky Balboa for Peter Farrelly's biopic.
articles.body: Anthony Ippolito's transformation into Sylvester Stallone for "I Play Rocky" didn't happen overnight. Ippolito, 27, packed on the pounds and overhauled his diet to portray the heavyweight boxer in the Peter Farrelly-directed biopic about the making of the Academy Award-winning film, "Rocky." The New York native explained how he endured "an entire lifestyle shift" before jumping in front of the camera to film "I Play Rocky," which follows Stallone's pursuit to bring Rocky Balboa to life on the big screen — a movie Stallone not only wrote in a few days as a struggling actor, but also refused to sell to a major studio unless he played the starring role. JOHN MADDEN ROLE PUSHES NICOLAS CAGE TO DRAMATIC PHYSICAL TRANSFORMATION WITH ‘BRUTAL’ DIET, PROSTHETICS "I had to gain a bunch of weight," Ippolito told Fox News Digital of his incredible transformation to play the boxer, which included the main priority of "eating a ton of food" every day before focusing on his actual diet and training. WATCH HERE: ‘I PLAY ROCKY' STAR ANTHONY IPPOLITO TRANSFORMS INTO SYLVESTER STALLONE "So, because knowing Stallone was playing Rocky, who is a heavyweight boxer in the movie, and he was a huge fan of Steve Reeves growing up," Ippolito explained of his preparation for becoming Rocky Balboa. SYLVESTER STALLONE CALLS HIMSELF AN 'IDIOT' FOR DOING HIS OWN STUNTS, DETAILS NINE BACK SURGERIES Reeves was known for enduring multiple full-body workouts per week to not only create, but also maintain his fighting physique, and prior to starring in the '58 Italian classic "Hercules," Reeves was credited with bringing bodybuilding to a global level as Mr. America in 1947, followed by Mr. Universe in 1950. Ippolito gained more than 30 pounds and spent months weightlifting and training in a boxing gym while also learning Stallone's specific dialect to transform into Rocky Balboa. "Stallone started weightlifting at a really young age, so he always had some type of physique," Ippolito said. Advertisement "It's something that's a really recognizable part of 'Rocky,' and I kind of knew I had to be there, so it was an entire lifestyle shift, to be honest with you." SYLVESTER STALLONE'S ADVICE TO THOSE WHO ARE STRUGGLING 50 YEARS AFTER 'ROCKY' CHANGED HIS LIFE Ippolito's transformation completely astounded the Academy Award winner, who admitted that he had "mixed" feelings about the film but was ultimately blown away by his character. While promoting his memoir, "The Steps," earlier this year, The Hollywood Reporter noted how Stallone grappled with the idea of the biopic and was initially "kind of mixed because I'm going, 'I’m not dead yet. Aren’t we jumping the gun a little bit?'" "And then I saw this video of this kid [Ippolito]. I actually thought it was me the first moment; there were a couple of angles. I go to my daughter and say, 'That’s unbelievable.'" PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE Ippolito was equally blown away by the compliment from the "Rocky" mastermind, and admitted "it's really, really unbelievable, very surreal." "And it means so much, because obviously, especially throughout making this, I only became a bigger fan of his in terms of what he was able to persevere through," Ippolito said. "It's just, it's kind of incredible. And so hearing him say that is really, really, really cool." After a back-and-forth with producers and ultimately denying himself a massive payout to sell the film prior to its creation, Stallone banked on himself to create the '76 flick with a $1 million budget. Behind-the-scenes production comes to life in Peter Farrelly's "I Play Rocky," where crews piece together a big-idea movie with relatively low funds and arguably over-the-top dreams. The director explained how Balboa's laser-focused Hollywood pursuit in the '70s wasn't too far off from the Tinseltown of today. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? articles.title: AICWA urges CM Devendra Fadnavis to curb Mumbai gangsters death threats to Saif Ali Khan and other celebs, firing at Tiger Shroff, issues warning: 'Shootings will stop completely'
articles.summary: The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) has asked Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis to step in as threats to film stars grow.
articles.body: The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) has asked Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis to step in as threats to film stars grow. The appeal comes days after Saif Ali Khan reportedly received a death threat, and it seeks tighter security for the actor and others in the industry.Several celebrities have been targeted by gangsters lately, and Tiger Shroff even had shots fired at him in public. Saif’s threat, which reportedly warned him of meeting the same fate as Baba Siddique, has now pushed the film body to act.What the letter to the CM saysAICWA president Suresh Shyamlal Gupta sent the letter to the chief minister and marked a copy to Mumbai police commissioner Deven Bharti. He pointed out that gangsters have openly threatened many actors in recent weeks and have claimed to have 200 shooters ready. The body cautioned that continued fear could start disrupting film shoots.A portion of the letter read, “The livelihood of lakhs of workers, technicians, artists and set workers is now at risk. If this continues, a lock will fall on Bollywood: shootings will stop completely, workers will lose their jobs and producers will suffer heavy losses.” It added, “Bollywood contributes significantly to the nation’s revenue and carries India’s name across the world. Every such incident damages that reputation. Because film personalities are visible and seen as soft targets, gangsters attack them for publicity and extortion.”Five demands put forwardSaying the situation feels like the 1990s, when the underworld held the industry in its grip, AICWA listed five demands. Some of them read, “Stronger security for Saif Ali Khan, Shri Amitabh Bachchan, Abhishek Bachchan and their families. Safety for all film personalities and filmmakers in Mumbai. Adequate police protection at all shooting locations.”The remaining demands were, “Strict action against gangsters and their networks, and a gangster-free Mumbai. Close monitoring of press conferences and public events involving film personalities.” The association also wrote, “Bollywood must be able to move freely on Mumbai’s streets, shoot and work without fear.”Police probe Saif Ali Khan’s threatMumbai Police told news agency PTI on Thursday that an investigation has begun into the alleged threat to Saif, and that its authenticity is being checked. A police official was quoted as saying, “Actor Saif Ali Khan received a voice message on his phone in the name of Zeeshan Akhtar, stating that he would meet the same fate as Baba Siddique.”Other stars on the radarAmitabh Bachchan, Ayushmann Khurrana, Diljit Dosanjh and Tusshar Kapoor have also received similar threats in recent weeks. Tiger was fired at in Juhu in October and escaped without injury, although his driver and a passerby were hurt by bullets. Salman Khan, meanwhile, has long faced threats from Lawrence Bishnoi and his gang in connection with an alleged blackbuck poaching case.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Let’s talk about GTA VI
articles.summary: Grand Theft Auto 6 has launched on the PS5 and Xbox, and Verge staff are discussing everything about the open-world game.
articles.body: It’s hard to believe, but Grand Theft Auto VI is now a real thing that we all can play. Thirteen years after GTA V, and eight years since Red Dead Redemption 2, Rockstar is back with its latest sprawling, extravagant open world. There’s a lot to experience — and a lot to talk about. Perhaps the most impressive thing about GTA VI is how flexible it is, letting you mold the experience to your own play style. You can still be a maniacal criminal, but you can also focus on the new love story that includes an entire button dedicated to holding hands. Or you can spend the hours fishing or driving around listening to the radio. Maybe you just want to doomscroll through a fake version of Instagram. As GTA VI producer Rob Nelson told me just ahead of launch, “It’s a risk. It’s a real change for Grand Theft Auto. You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.” Now that the game is out and people are finding their own way through Leonida, it’s a great time to start talking about it. I’ve played through the entire main story — you can read my review right here — but I’m nowhere close to experiencing everything in the game. But I’m happy to answer any questions you have, though I’ll be careful around some of the big story spoilers. I’ll also be joined by senior reporter Jay Peters, who is still early in the game and can offer a different perspective. There’s a good chance some other Verge staff will stop by as well, since we’re basically all playing it. So drop all of your questions, theories, and stray thoughts about GTA VI here. I’ll be checking in throughout the day to join the conversation in the comments.

articles.title: New movies to watch this weekend: See 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' in theaters, rent or buy 'The Odyssey,' stream 'Madden' on Prime Video
articles.summary: The biggest movies opening this Nov. 20 weekend, from a new "Hunger Games" film to a story about Sylvester Stallone.
articles.body:
It's been 11 years since the last Katniss Everdeen-fronted Hunger Games movie ( Mockingjay — Part 2 ) came out, and three since the series' first cinematic prequel (2023's The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes ) opened. Now fans of the franchise can sink their teeth into a second prequel, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping , starring East of Eden 's Joseph Zada as a young Haymitch Abernathy, the role played by Woody Harrelson in the original films.

It's by far the buzziest film release for the Nov. 20 weekend, but don't sleep on I Play Rocky or Paper Tiger as they expand nationwide in theaters. Over on streaming, Prime Video's Madden — starring Nicolas Cage as NFL legend John Madden — debuts. Surprise, surprise, I didn't think it was as bad as other critics did .

And if you somehow missed seeing The Odyssey in theaters (how!?), you can now make it a movie night at home. Christopher Nolan's Greek epic is newly available to rent or buy. And on streaming services you're likely already paying for, a disturbing drama that's an unsettling and uncomfortable experience but still worthwhile, Gentle Monster, now on Netflix.

And there's plenty more. Keep reading our latest Trust Me, I Watch Everything to see what's worth watching this Nov. 20 opening weekend.

The buzziest release: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

Why it's a mixed bag: There's nothing all that wrong with Sunrise on the Reaping, the sixth Hunger Games movie and the second prequel. It simply has the misfortune of coming on the heels of the franchise-resurrecting previous entry, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, which was far better than anyone expected a cash-grab sequel meant to resurrect lucrative franchise IP for a new generation to be. It had a unique, borderline musical take on the world of Panem, using song as a storytelling device.

But Sunrise on the Reaping shows the limits of the Hunger Games series as it jumps forward in time and loses the specificity of the musical take. The cast consists largely of younger versions of characters we've already met. At one point, it's Hunger Games: Babies.

The film is set 40 years after Ballad and 24 years before the original The Hunger Games, and starts on the morning of the reaping of the 50th Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell. We follow 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), who you may remember as Woody Harrelson's character.

Melodrama that would otherwise be affecting is dulled by sheer repetition. It's by-the-numbers fare with no surprises — young people who don't deserve to die, die, but the emotional investment is missing. You know where it's going at every turn.

It's full of clunky dialogue that explains itself, and pacing that does it no favors. By the time we finally get to the Games, we barely see any of the action, and 90% of the tributes die offscreen. As far as the "resistance" goes, it reiterates the messaging of previous entries that no matter how hard these kids try to buck the system, the system wins. Fighting back feels futile.

For all its faults, Sunrise on the Reaping is sturdy and well-made — director Francis Lawrence has now made five of these and certainly knows what he's doing — but at this point, it's clear these movies are continuing because they're still box office draws, not because there's more story to tell. It's better than it should be, given these conditions, but you feel the returns diminishing in real time.

What other critics are saying : Reviews are decent but mixed. The AP's Mark Kennedy writes, "Credit goes to screenwriters Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie for crafting an engrossing plot from Suzanne Collins's latest prequel novel, which is expertly paced by director Francis Lawrence." Amy Nicholson of the Los Angeles Times writes, "Honestly, after spending six movies with District 12's salt-of-the-earth types, I'd rather hang out with ridiculous Capitol residents like Kieran Culkin's Caesar Flickerman."

How to watch: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is now playing in theaters nationwide .

Why you should see it: Anthony Ippolito's performance as Sylvester Stallone is so uncanny, there are a few shots in the film where your mind actually tricks you into believing you're watching archival footage of Stallone making Rocky. Stallone's manner of speaking and entire persona are so distinctive that a sustained impersonation shouldn't work, but Ippolito sells it so well, it's not a problem at all.

Rocky is one of the greatest and most rousing crowd-pleasing underdog stories of all time, so making a movie about it is kind of a cheat code already . But what really makes it sing is that Stallone's journey to get Rocky — and himself — on the big screen is an underdog story in its own right.

The movie starts with Stallone calling himself Mike. He's an unknown actor with an unshakable belief that he wasn't just meant to write Rocky — he was meant to be Rocky Balboa. Told "no" at every turn, Stallone bets everything on himself, holding the line on playing the lead against seemingly impossible odds.

Much of the movie's drive comes from the negotiations with the studio, which is doing everything in its power to make Rocky without Stallone in the lead role, while the actor remains indignant, saying he won't let them. Everyone thinks he's a madman, but it's that belief in himself and his refusal to give up on his dream that make the movie so affecting and effective. There's a poetic poignancy here, even if the movie gets a little repetitive with the back-and-forth of "this guy won't play Rocky" and "this guy must play Rocky."

Ultimately, Ippolito sells the hell out of it. It's charming!

What other critics are saying : They like it! David Rooney at The Hollywood Reporter writes, "The element that holds the movie together is Ippolito, who nails the garbled, rumbling diction, hangdog expression and hulking physicality of Stallone while never losing sight of his insecurities at this unproven point in his career." Variety's Owen Gleiberman writes, "The pleasure of I Play Rocky is that it understands the karmic way in which the story of Rocky — the underdog who triumphs against all odds — was echoed in the saga of how Stallone got the movie off the ground."

How to watch: I Play Rocky is now playing in theaters nationwide.

Why you should see it: Auteur James Gray ( Little Odessa, We Own the Night, Armageddon Time ) is back with yet another crime thriller about family, the Russian mob and growing up in Queens.

Two brothers (Miles Teller and Adam Driver) become entangled in a scheme that turns out to be too good to be true. As they try to navigate their way through the dangerous world of the Russian mafia, family bonds begin to fray, with life-altering consequences.

This description could describe a number of Gray's films, but Paper Tiger — much like Wild Horse Nine , in which filmmaker Martin McDonagh iterates on a theme to great effect — feels like Gray finally making the movie he's been trying to make his whole career. It's a tense family melodrama that just so happens to feature the mafia and will certainly end in tragedy.

At first glance, it's grounded and seemingly low-stakes; eventually, you realize that's not true. It's a rich work that culminates with a breathtaking sequence of violence that will have you questioning what you learned from it.

What other critics are saying: Reviews are a little all over the place, but some came away impressed. AP's Lindsay Bahr writes, "It builds to one of the more thrilling and inventive showdowns in recent film history — a rare movie that embraces, rather than tries to disguise, the omnipresent sound of planes taking off and landing at a nearby airport." Owen Gleiberman at Variety wasn't as charmed, writing, "You can feel James Gray wanting to will something like a Lumet version of Greek tragedy. ... But even the scene-to-scene skill of Gray's direction can't stop the movie from turning into a mixture of the grandiose and the implausible."

How to watch: Paper Tiger is now playing in theaters nationwide .

Why you should watch it: Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey delivers everything you'd want from an epic of this size and scale, and then some. But it also functions as a spiritual sequel to Oppenheimer , continuing Nolan's psychological examination of men reflecting on their roles in destructive moments that changed the world.

Oppenheimer was about the invention of the nuclear bomb and the torment of the scientist behind its creation at the destruction it wrought. Nolan's The Odyssey is an anti-war epic about Odysseus (Matt Damon, in a career-best performance) reckoning with the trauma and horrors of war. It also specifically explores how breaking Zeus's Law — which boils down to the golden rule of "treat others the way you'd want to be treated," with the added caveat of "because the gods are hiding among humans and you don't want to mistreat one" — has led to the breakdown of a civil society.

Despite the trappings and budget of a blockbuster spectacle — which it absolutely is — The Odyssey is also an achingly human film. Underneath all the swords, arrows and monsters, it's deeply moving. The ensemble cast is terrific and also surprising; Himesh Patel stands out for having a role far larger than some of his A-list co-stars, and Samantha Morton really makes the most of her brief time onscreen.

What other critics are saying: It's earned lavish praise pretty much all around. Clarisse Loughrey at the Independent writes, "This is a blockbuster of literally unprecedented scale. It is also Nolan's best work to date. It deserves to be the film that defines him." AV Club's Monica Castillo adds that "Nolan takes a familiar story and filters it through many of his obsessions, like time-jumping through events and focusing on the lonely hero in the throes of a tortured journey, both making this translation uniquely his."

How to watch: The Odyssey is now available to rent or buy on Apple TV , Prime Video and other VOD platforms.

What to know: If you haven't heard of the legendary Toronto production of Godspell, this joyful and funny documentary will tell you all you need to know. The story goes that Martin Short, Eugene Levy, Gilda Radner, Victor Garber, Paul Shaffer and other entertainment icons got their start in the 1972 show, which was so transcendently funny that it became the stuff of legend for fans of comedy and theater. This documentary features interviews with the surviving cast members, plus Lin-Manuel Miranda, Mike Myers and more, recounting a pivotal moment in comedy history in great detail. You feel like you are, in fact, there, despite there being very little footage of the production itself.

How to watch: Available to rent or buy on Apple TV , Prime Video and other VOD platforms.

📺 Movies newly available on streaming services you may already have

Why it's a mixed bag: The badness of this new David O. Russell movie has been comically overstated . Not to say that it's particularly good — it isn't — but it's clearly going for comedy in a way that some people are oblivious to.

It brings to mind the comedies of Adam McKay and Will Ferrell — this is David O. Russell's Talladega Nights, a broad satire about America, or Step Brothers with John Madden and Al Davis in the roles meant for Ferrell and John C. Reilly. The problem here is just how broad it is, and the tone is never really consistent.

The film chronicles John Madden's (Nicolas Cage) journey alongside his best friend and true original Al Davis (Christian Bale) — from a Super Bowl-winning partnership with the Raiders, to becoming football's most recognizable voice, to building the worldwide Madden NFL video game.

The movie is at its best, and funniest, when it's just a "two guys being dudes" bromance between Madden and Davis. Bale and Cage, both actors known for their fierce commitment to roles, are indeed really going for it — including Cage gaining some weight but still wearing a fat suit — and it's fun to watch them goof around. But it does have more of an SNL sketch energy than that of a feature-film biopic with anything to say about the man. Kathryn Hahn is always fun to watch, but it feels like she's in a more traditional movie than everybody else.

Simply put, there's just not much to Madden , and it feels as if it's moving at such a frenetic pace to mask that fact. It's an easy watch, but it's also clear why this ended up debuting unceremoniously on Prime on a Wednesday instead of in theaters across the country.

What other critics are saying : They hate it! G. Allen Johnson at the San Francisco Chronicle writes, "If Madden were a football game, it would be an offensively challenged contest, filled with turnovers and penalties, the kind of performance that could get coaches fired. In other words, the opposite of the Raiders teams Madden coached in the 1970s." The Guardian's Andrew Lawrence adds, "Russell's Madden is closer to the Pop Tarts movie version of the formidable coach's story than Ben Affleck's Air , reducing one of the 20th century's most celebrated pop culture figures to a thin caricature."

How to watch: Madden is now streaming on Prime Video .

Why you should watch it: Léa Seydoux is extraordinary in this disturbing drama about a woman, Lucy, discovering that her husband and the father of her child is charged with possession of child sexual abuse material.

Filmmaker Marie Kreutzer expands the scope of the film as we follow the female police officer assigned to the case and see the troubles she herself is having with her aging father.

The film seems to suggest that there's no such thing as a "good man" and that monstrous, evil behavior can lurk in both the most unexpected places and the most normal-seeming people.

It reminded me a bit of You Can See Everything, the movie of the moment, in that it's ultimately about the unknowability of others. It's an unsettling and uncomfortable viewing experience.

What other critics are saying: It's well-reviewed! Tim Grierson of the Los Angeles Times writes, "Lucy's behavior may be frustratingly inconsistent, but many viewers will recognize the immeasurable suffering that drives it." Natalie Keogan at AV Club writes, "An actress comfortable with wading in nuance and uncertainty, it's unsurprising that Seydoux is uniquely equipped for such a role."

What to know: It's as if Enchanted and Shrek had a baby! Cinderella's evil stepsister, Lilith (voiced by Ali Wong), steals the Fairy Godmother's (Bette Midler) wand and shatters the story as we know it — dooming the kingdom to the tyrannical rule of the villainous Priscilla (Nikki Glaser). Now, Lilith must team up with Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried) to save the kingdom. Steps is in familiar territory as a self-aware revisionist modern fairy tale send-up, but it carves just enough of its own path to recommend, and the cast is insanely stacked.

How to watch: Now streaming on Netflix .

What to know: Canadian filmmaker Matt Johnson ( Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie, BlackBerry ) leaps into the mainstream with Tony , a melancholy yet always charming coming-of-age dramedy. It also happens to be a biopic about Anthony Bourdain, loosely adapted from his breakthrough book, Kitchen Confidential . In it, a 19-year-old Bourdain travels to Provincetown and stumbles into the chaotic world of a restaurant kitchen, setting off a summer that will shape the course of his life. The movie opens with a quote from the book: "I was — to be frank — a spoiled, miserable, narcissistic, self-destructive and thoughtless young lout, and badly in need of a good ass-kicking." In this movie, he gets that ass-kicking. But does it help? Dominic Sessa, the breakout star of The Holdovers, is transcendent here, perfectly embodying Bourdain and the specific way he speaks, without ever feeling like he's doing a cheap imitation or impression. It's such a brooding portrayal and appropriately gloomy without ever crossing into discomfort, given that the audience is likely aware of how Bourdain's story ends. Tony is more of a hangout movie with an unbeatable vibe than a traditional life-to-death biopic. There's just a warmth to everything here, from the texture of the photography to its characters. Read my full review here .

How to watch: Now streaming on HBO Max .

We'll see you next week, just in time for the big Thanksgiving releases.

articles.title: Robert Pattinson’s Bond Ascent: How Pricey Screen Tests and Amazon Execs Landed a Starry 007
articles.summary: What does an actor do in the quiet moments before the announcement that will change his life? For Robert Pattinson, there were about 12 hours between the Sun...
articles.body:
What does an actor do in the quiet moments before the announcement that will change his life?

For Robert Pattinson, there were about 12 hours between the Sunday phone call confirming he'd landed the role of James Bond and Amazon MGM's Monday-morning release of the first image of the actor rocking a tuxedo and pistol. He spent it, rather predictably, watching an arthouse horror film.

His longtime friend and collaborator Robert Eggers told Variety this week that Pattinson was screening the director's forthcoming genre drama "Werwulf" when the Bond news broke. Nothing like a stark naked Aaron Taylor-Johnson terrorizing a quaint village to pass the time.

But after months (years, really) of toiling and speculation over who would replace Daniel Craig in the film adaptations of Ian Fleming's spy novels, Pattinson took the crown. It buttons up a delicious, messy and very public guessing game over which lucky man would land the iconic role. When Amazon MGM bought out rights to James Bond from longtime custodians the Broccoli family in 2025, intentions were set for a young star who could shoulder the franchise for a decade or two. An A-list team of producers (Amy Pascal of "Spider-Man" and David Heyman of the "Harry Potter" movies) recruited Denis Villeneuve to direct. Together, with significant influence from Amazon execs Courtenay Valenti and Mike Hopkins (and yes, Jeff Bezos), they screen-tested a laundry list of virile performers — including Callum Turner, Tom Francis, Jack Lowden and Josh O'Connor — earlier this year.

For the curious, the batch of screen tests cost Amazon MGM between $300,000 and $500,000 to pull off, ostensibly in secret (everyone found out), sources familiar with the process say. But two wildcard actors who tested at the last minute — "Superman" star Nicholas Hoult and the DCU's reining Batman, Pattinson — tipped the scales. Villeneuve's voice became the most trusted in the room on the matter of Bond's casting, two insiders tell Variety .

His shorthand with Pattinson from working on "Dune: Part Three" made the choice inevitable, according to industry insiders — especially after Turner, the early favorite, came under scrutiny against more established names like Hoult and Pattinson. Lowden, the heat-seeking star of "Slow Horses," was even the subject of a suspected sabotage campaign when paparazzi footage circulated showed the actor bungling an on-set motorcycle stunt just two weeks before the Bond casting was confirmed.

A sect of the internet lost its mind when Variety reported earlier this month that Harry Styles and Theo James were both in talks for the role. It's rare, even by tentpole movie standards, that such a long list of candidates would flow so freely through public channels. The studios hate it because it makes them seem indecisive, one exec says. Talent absolutely hates it because the also-rans will have to answer for almost being James Bond on talk show couches and podcasts for the next 10 years.

"Whatever, it's really fun," one top talent rep tells Variety of the audition merry-go-round.

While there will be detractors, it's inarguable that the Bond gig now enshrines Pattinson in the upper echelons of movie stardom. He was already well on his way, with even civilian social media pundits having commented on the "generational run" Pattinson has been living out onscreen in films like "Primetime," "The Odyssey," "The Drama," "Die My Love" and, obviously, "The Batman." That's to say nothing of the deeply indie era ("Good Time," "The Lighthouse") that followed major franchise moments like his star-making turn in the "Twilight Saga" movies and a prominent role in "Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire." The new job also represents a major win for Pattinson's agent of more than 20 years, Stephanie Ritz of WME. Ritz and team have managed to populate massive IP with Pattinson's face while still allowing the actor to take risks and brand himself a maverick for the cross-generational devotees of studios like A24.

Given the shocking November news that DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran had been jettisoned by the David Ellison regime, it's doubtful Pattinson would linger long as Matt Reeves' caped crusader — freeing him up to embody the sultry British charm and execute the bare-knuckle action audiences have come to expect from 007. Art-house horror movies may have to take a back seat.

articles.title: Lance Broadway, former MLB pitcher turned actor, dies in apartment complex stairwell
articles.summary: Former MLB pitcher and actor Lance Broadway died this week, according to the Dallas County Medical Examiner’s Office.
articles.body: Former MLB pitcher and actor Lance Broadway died this week, according to the Dallas County Medical Examiner’s Office. He was 43. The medical examiner lists Broadway’s manner of death as “pending,” but indicates that he died in the stairwell of an apartment complex off Lemon Avenue, near Dallas-Love Field Airport. The Bryan native had deep ties to North Texas, attending Grand Prairie and Waxahachie high schools before playing college baseball at TCU and Dallas Baptist. In 2005, he was named to the Conference USA All-Tournament Team and was also named pitcher of the year and Male Athlete of the Year. He was drafted by the Chicago White Sox with the 15th overall pick in the first round of the 2005 MLB Draft. Broadway made his major league debut with the White Sox in 2007. He appeared in 27 MLB games for Chicago and he played for the New York Mets from 2007 to 2009. After his baseball career, Broadway pursued acting, appearing in the 2013 film “Olympus Has Fallen” and television series including “Lucifer,” “Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.” and “Colony.” The Dallas County Medical Examiner’s Office has not determined Broadway’s manner of death. Dallas police have a case number associated with the death, but additional information about the circumstances was not immediately available.

articles.title: Andrey Zvyagintsev believes filmmakers know what the audience wants — not executives
articles.summary: The director of Minotaur says there is no politics in Russia.
articles.body: The year is 2022. Vladimir Putin has announced the military draft. In Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur, set in the fictional town of Krasoborsk, a quietly unhappy couple, called Gleb and Galina, carry on with their lives, or try to, geopolitics notwithstanding. For Galina, carrying on means an affair, which we deduce from a scene of her texting with a faint smile, her face lit in the dark by the light of her phone. (Minotaur is a remake of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 film The Unfaithful Wife, whose title gives the plot away more readily than Zvyagintsev’s.) Meanwhile, Gleb runs a kind of private contracting concern and is soon asked to scare up military recruits to meet a quota. At this point, the domestic noir and the workplace drama merge to dramatic, devastating, and darkly funny effects. In Minotaur, as in his five other features, Zvyagintsev has the camera moving seemingly objectively, almost omnisciently, putting the characters in their context. Occasionally they appear rather small, especially when set against the epic scale of their mythic and biblical fates. That the environment shapes the person seems to be a recurring revelation across all six of his staggering films. Minotaur, too, opens with a natural landscape of the arboreal kind and ends with another, different landscape, of clouds. In the middle is a movie about people trying to make sense of the landscapes they find themselves in, of the social, moral, relational variety. Zvyagintsev has some experience with finding oneself in incomprehensible landscapes. After receiving Russia’s Sputnik V covid-19 vaccine during the pandemic, he fell ill, and later learned about the invasion of Ukraine while recovering from a medical coma in Germany. He subsequently chose not to return home, moving to France. At the Cannes Film Festival in May, Minotaur won the second-highest honor. In his acceptance speech, Zvyagintsev spoke about the war, saying: “The only person who can stop this butchery is the President of the Russian Federation. Put an end to this carnage. The whole world is waiting for it.” While he resists the identity of exile, in September the Russian government designated him a “foreign agent.” [Image: Minotaur is based on Chabrol’s The Unfaithful Wife. Zvyagintsev returned this year to the New York Film Festival, where he last visited with his 2014 film Leviathan, which won a Golden Globe and was nominated for an Oscar. His debut in 2003, The Return, won a top prize at Venice International Film Festival, after which he was invited to meet Putin, an account of which appears in his forthcoming book. Out of his six films, four have won prestigious prizes at Cannes, including Elena and Loveless. We discussed the three years he spent cleaning the streets of Moscow in the early 1990s, his status as a Russian immigrant in France now, and how he captures that great Chekhovian instinct: that life is wretched, but what can we do, we must go on living. Zvyagintsev spoke to The Verge through a translator from Los Angeles. I understand you went from cleaning streets to making commercials. What happened in between? It kind of happened almost at the same time, because I was cleaning the streets to be able to live in Moscow. From 1990 to 1993, I was cleaning the streets. And then I was going to the Museum of Cinema and watching a movie every single day. Those were my formative years, when I learned a lot about cinema. And then I was let go. I had been living in a huge communal flat, free accommodation in a beautiful historic mansion in central Moscow. It was a really big apartment, and there were three street cleaners, including me, that lived there. In 1993, I was forced to leave the apartment after someone from the local housing administration decided to take it over. The two others had families, so they decided that if someone was supposed to move, it was going to be me, since I was single. I was offered alternative accommodation, but realized that the only reason I had continued working as a street sweeper was to keep that particular apartment. So the first night when I had to leave the apartment, I left it fast without an actual plan. I had to spend the night inside a truck that was abandoned and that was parked in the street. I got a new job as a guard, as a night guard at a kindergarten where I also ate leftover food from the children’s meals. After the first day, I called my friend who was working in commercials and doing music videos. I asked him to help with a job, because I was sure I was able to shoot commercials. After the first commercial, I met some producers who liked my work, and then I started shooting commercials on the regular and working as a freelance for some time. One of those commercials was noticed by a producer from a TV channel called REN TV, who was shooting a bunch of TV series at the time. His name was Dmitry Lesnevsky and he asked me whether I wanted to shoot movies, and I said it was my dream. And then Dmitry presented me with 15 scripts of choice, and I shot three episodes of a television series called The Black Room for this channel, each 25 minutes long. How did you know this friend? We were army friends. He was a close friend from the army. He was a cinema mechanic. He was starting movies for the soldiers when they were in the army. They had a theater, and I was in the music ensemble in the army. He was also an actor. You had an adverse reaction to a covid vaccine. You were ill for a long time. You nearly died. You moved, and eventually settled in France. You’ve said you can’t know how that experience changed you as a filmmaker, but I’m curious if you know how that experience changed you as a person. I got sick in Russia. I was in a coma for 40 days in Germany. I had a major problem with my lungs, a bacteria called klebsiella found its way there. They thought that they would need a lung transplant. Fortunately, the Germans were able to operate, and the transplant was not needed. I moved to France a year later after the coma. What was the biggest change for me was the rhythm of life. I understood that you cannot lose time, so I’m trying to do things in a much more dynamic manner, and not leave things for later because we don’t know if this later exists. So that that’s the biggest change, really, just seeing life as something that passes by quickly. You are a vocal opponent of the current Russian government. Do you consider yourself to be in political exile? I am not in political exile. I did not have that status, and I never applied for it because I don’t see any necessity for that. I consider myself an immigrant. I’ve been living away from my native country for almost five years, but I did not leave on purpose. I was already in Europe when the war happened. There is a term in Russian, called nevozvrashchenets, which means a person who does not come back, someone who has left their home country and has not returned, particularly for political reasons. I was in the clinic in Germany and then in France when the war started, and I realized that I could not go back to the country that is at war. You’ve said you are not political, but your movies seem overtly political, to me. You’ve also said that the job of an artist is to reflect reality. You don’t think you’re political, but your job is to reflect reality, and we are living at a time when politics is dominant. How do you reconcile all this? It’s very simple to reconcile. It’s just that the politics barges into our lives, and we have to reflect what’s going on in the world. You become a witness of what’s going on beyond your window, what’s going on to the environment, to the world around you, to the world close to you. It just so happens that the politics dominate our lives. We are witnessing historical events that we cannot not reflect in the movies. When I say I’m not a political animal, I mean that I have no way of influencing the political process in my country, especially while the war is going on. There is no politics in Russia, in the sense of politics being a struggle for power, dialogue between different parties or worldviews, you know, left, right, Democrats, Republicans. This does not exist in Russia. There’s only one power. It feels more like domination in the way Foucault meant it. Yes. It’s not even that there is only one party that dominates. It’s that no one even questions it, and no one even tries to struggle. It’s kind of a totalitarian regime at this time. Let’s talk Minotaur. I believe you said you wanted to adapt Ingrid Bergman first, but when that didn’t go, you asked your producers for other available properties and they sent you a list. You also said you asked for marital dramas from the ’60s and ’70s specifically. Why? I wanted to do a remake of a movie that would have three or four main characters, not a lot of different locations, that would be a little more compact, because there was a certain budget consideration. The films that I had previously considered, the scripts I considered, were more expensive, and so I was not able to get any of them going. And that’s when I asked for the list from my friend who is French, and he gave me a list of French films. If I had an Italian friend, those would have been Italian movies. I asked him for the best films from the ’60s and ’70s because it’s far away enough for us, those were probably the films that were a little bit more forgotten by the public, or a new generation of the public maybe hasn’t seen them. And that’s how I discovered Claude Chabrol’s The Unfaithful Wife. You also said that something about the Chabrol did not work for you, and that’s what gave you the inspiration to want to remake it. I wouldn’t formulate it as something not working, but I would rather say that he made a kind of a formal choice when it comes to the office life of the main character. Chabrol concentrates more on the crime plot and the love triangle [than the office life], which is totally his right. And I thought it was something that I would like to fill in. In 2022, the war was going on, and then in September they started the partial mobilization in Russia, and so this plot kind of just barged into our movie, and filled out that space that was empty previously. Your movies are full of scenes Hollywood executives would ask to cut. I am thinking of the ending of Minotaur, with the clouds, or The Banishment, which ends with women collecting hay and they are singing. What is the effect of these moments in your movies? It would be impossible to cut out those moments. What are they doing in the movie? When you say that Hollywood execs would probably like to cut that stuff out, the viewers, including viewers in Hollywood, really like the clouds [that Minotaur ends on], for example, and they even tell me that the sequence could have been longer. So I want to tell you that the execs do not know what the viewers want because when the viewer goes to the cinema, he kind of goes to sleep and then he watches a dream. And as long as this dream is aesthetically pleasing and harmonious and beautiful, that’s what the viewers should be watching, and no one should cut that out. This is the key conflict between the producer and the creator. The producer does not trust the creator to know what the audience wants, but the creator knows. And so, if the producer is so sure of himself, he should write a script himself. You published a book about the making of your third film, Elena. I understand you’re working on a second book. What can you tell us about this project? Will it include advice to young filmmakers? The whole book, in a way, will be an advice to younger filmmakers, or people who love movies, because it will be a very detailed account of the six films that I have released so far, six conversations with one of the best cinema critics writing in Russian, Anton Dolin. Would you ever work in another language apart from Russian or with Netflix? Yes, I am open. In fact, I have a script in English. Two even.

articles.title: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B
articles.summary: Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it looks like Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain.
articles.body:
Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit.

Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.

Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the new cash will be used to repurchase shares.

Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.

Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the company has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro . Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.

“We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July .

articles.title: Boys Noize turns to the club (and an obscure Italian synth) for inspiration on 7LLVSION
articles.summary: Boys Noize says his new album, 7LLVSION, is ’tech-driven … I always look for the newest machines.’
articles.body: If you’re wondering how Alex Ridha’s (aka Boys Noize) collaboration with Nine Inch Nails influenced his new record 7LLVSION, the answer is simple: It didn’t. That’s not to say Ridha didn’t learn anything from the virtuosic production team of Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, but most of the songs on 7LLVSION had been knocking around for some time. And as Ridha is quick to point out, these are not rock songs built for live performance; they’re “battle tested” for clubs and DJ sets. “I was kind of back on the usual kind of thing,” he tells The Verge. “I do the same I kind of always do. I go make coffee, go in my room, put on the machines, and I’ll start messing around with sounds and build one sound to another and there comes a record,” he says. Like previous Boys Noize releases, a lot of 7LLVSION starts with sound design. “It’s kind of tech-driven, in a way,” he says, “because I always look for the newest machines.” On 7LLVSION, Ridha frequently turned to an obscure Italian semimodular synth, the Grp A4. “It’s just so powerful, and it sounds so big,” he says. The routing options, dual filters (which he uses in parallel), and built-in sequencer kept leading him to new and inspiring places. Because of that, the A4 ended up on a number of tracks, including “Shut It Down,” “1+1+1,” and “Ycore.”. [Media: “The exciting part is always to, you know, not repeat myself, even with the drum sounds, and try something new that I haven’t tried before,” Ridha says. For a few tracks, that meant getting away from the rigid, quantized grooves of techno and opting for a more dynamic, live feeling on tracks like “Shut It Down” and “1+1+1” especially. “Live drums are the new 808,” he says. He looked to German bands of the ’70s and ’80s for inspiration, like Can, Amon Düül, and Deutsch Amerikanische Freundschaft. He also called out Conny Plank, who produced landmark records by Neu!, Kraftwerk, and Eurythmics. But in general he says, “My goal is to not sound like anything you can point to. You know, I don’t want to be a direct copy.” Instead, he was chasing the sound of “electronic punk.” That means aggressive basslines, driving drums, and stripped-down arrangements that avoid overstuffing the mix with too many instruments. But it all comes back to the club at the end of the day. “Environment has always been the main thing in my music. I need to have a record that I want to play at the party,” he says, and that meant testing the songs off 7LLVSION extensively in his DJ sets and letting the audience tell him what works and what doesn’t. “The club is the most open and objective situation you can have,” he says. “They don’t know what I’m playing, so they hear something for the first time, and you can just look at someone’s face, or someone’s there in the room to get a cool reaction, and that usually makes me feel good about something or not.” Boys Noize is currently touring the world on the festival circuit, and 7LLVSION is available now on most major streaming services.

articles.title: Darius Rucker says he used to drink a bottle of whiskey a day during wild Hootie & the Blowfish years
articles.summary: Darius Rucker admits drinking a bottle of whiskey a day on the road as Hootie & the Blowfish fame fueled substance abuse in new Hulu documentary.
articles.body: Darius Rucker's meteoric rise to fame as the lead singer of Hootie & the Blowfish was captured in the latest Hulu documentary, "They Called Me Hootie." Breaking onto the scene in the early '90s, the group of college friends from South Carolina broke records with "Cracked Rear View" released in 1994, but fame and fortune came at a cost and Rucker soon spiraled into substance abuse and drinking issues at the peak of the band's popularity. Rucker, 60, admitted that at one point he was drinking one bottle of whiskey per day while on the road, and casual drug use became routine. BRAD PITT SAYS HE CAN DRINK IN ‘RESTRAINED MANNER’ AFTER 7 SOBER YEARS, BUT EXPERT RAISES RED FLAG "I smoked a little pot," Rucker said. "If we had a day over, someone would get some acid." After the band upgraded to a tour bus, things took a drastic detour. "One day, I came back to our bus, I walked in the back and two of the guys were lining up some cocaine," Rucker said. "And the party just was on from that point." ‘BACK TO THE FUTURE’ STAR CHRISTOPHER LLOYD CONFESSES HE WAS ‘HOOKED’ ON COCAINE DURING ‘TAXI’ YEARS He added, "We earned our reputation. We went crazy, man. It was rock and roll." Rucker recalled once buying trash bags full of mushrooms from someone on the bus. "I'm like, 'Mushrooms? Really? How many mushrooms you got?' 'We've got two garbage bags of mushrooms,'" he said. "And he's like, 'Well, we're probably gonna make about $45,000.' It’s like, 'What if we give you [$30,000] right now?' articles.title: Vin Diesel steps away from ‘Fast & Furious’ and ‘Guardians of the Galaxy’ for his original action film ‘Burial Hill’, makers close in on a USD 35 million to USD 40 million deal for international rights
articles.summary: Vin Diesel is moving away from the ‘Fast & Furious’ and ‘Guardians of the Galaxy’ worlds to headline an original action thriller called ‘Burial Hill’.
articles.body: Vin Diesel is moving away from the ‘Fast & Furious’ and ‘Guardians of the Galaxy’ worlds to headline an original action thriller called ‘Burial Hill’. The makers want to turn it into a fresh franchise, and makers are reportedly finalising a big deal for the international rights.According to the Deadline report, Vin Diesel is joining hands with writer Mike McGrale, who penned the upcoming ‘John Wick’ spinoff ‘Caine’, and director Jamie Payne. The filmmaker is known for helming both Netflix ‘Luther’ films and the original Idris Elba series, along with episodes of ‘Outlander’, ‘The Alienist’ and ‘Doctor Who’.What is ‘Burial Hill’ about?Vin Diesel plays a reclusive groundskeeper with a hidden past. The story begins when a corrupt state police unit chases a young witness to their crimes right into the cemetery he calls home. He is then dragged back into the violent life he walked away from, as he tries to save her and take down the cops who want the truth buried. More cast members are being finalised.Studio closes in on international rightsThe project had been generating strong buzz behind the scenes in recent months. It could have been shown to buyers at the American Film Market, but heavy studio interest changed that plan.Amazon MGM Studios is now reportedly finalising a deal for most international territories, except a few such as CIS, and will hold all rights in those regions. The deal is said to be worth around USD 35 million to USD 40 million. It follows the studio’s early pre-buy of A24’s ‘Elden Ring’. Talks for a North American deal are also on, though the interested buyers are not yet known.Production plans and budgetMarc Butan, who produced ‘Plane’, will produce the film with Vin Diesel and Samantha Vincent’s One Race Films. Mad River’s Matt Berger will serve as executive producer.The film is being fast-tracked for a shoot in the first quarter of next year, most likely in Australia. Additional funding has been arranged by the producers, and the budget is said to be between USD 60 million and USD 70 million.A rare move for the action starIf filming goes ahead as planned, it will be Diesel’s first film outside Marvel and ‘Fast & Furious’ in six years and only the second in a decade. It is uncommon to see him step out of his hit franchises, which also include the ‘xXx’ films.The actor and producer is currently shooting ‘Fast Forever’, set for a 2028 release, and has also been named an executive producer on a ‘Fast & Furious’ TV series. Both are being made for Universal.The creative team’s recent workJamie Payne is in post-production on the second ‘Luther’ film with Idris Elba and recently directed multiple episodes of Apple’s ‘Star City’ and ‘Outlander: Blood of My Blood’. McGrale co-wrote the story for Netflix’s ‘The Rip’ and co-wrote the screenplay of Lionsgate’s ‘Caine’, which is directed by Donnie Yen. articles.title: Melania Trump Takes Brutal Swipe At Husband Donald For Having So Many ‘Yes People’ Around Him: ‘That’s Not Healthy’
articles.summary: Melania Trump is airing some details about her marriage in a revealing clip from her new docuseries, where she explains […]
articles.body:
Melania Trump is airing some details about her marriage in a revealing clip from her new docuseries, where she explains that Donald Trump finds her "difficult" because she tells him the truth, unlike people around him.

In her new two-part Amazon Prime docuseries, "Melania: The Series," the first lady explained that she's not one of the president's sycophants and also implied that spending some time away from him is essential for their marriage.

Melania's public appearances fell significantly during the president's second term, prompting increased speculation about the state of her marriage as she and Trump have reportedly become increasingly separate.

Melania Explains Her Surprising Dynamic With Husband Trump

The documentary, directed by Brett Ratner, premiered in New York City on Thursday night. In a clip shared by The Daily Beast , Melania explained that she has to tell Trump the truth because hardly anyone else would.

When asked who was a more "difficult" spouse, Trump noted that he was "very easy to get along with, actually, much easier than the public would understand." He added that Melania "could very well be more difficult than me."

Melania, in response, exposed that the president surrounds himself with many people who mindlessly agree with him, prompting her to sometimes be "difficult."

"He said, 'Oh, she's so difficult,' but I tell him the truth," she explained. "I feel that sometimes there are too many people around him, that they are 'yes people,' and that's not healthy."

Ratner also asked in a separate clip shared by The Beast what Melania learned from observing her parents, Viktor and Amalija Knavs, during their almost six-decade-long marriage.

She responded by framing her independence as part of the secret to a successful relationship. "You cannot spend [time] non-stop with that person," she says. "I think solitude is very important."

Melania elaborated, stating that it is necessary to let your partner be "who they are, and enjoy what they do, and not to be that they are overwhelmed with you and nagging all the time."

Melania Trump's Reduced Public Schedule During Her Husband's Second Term

The first lady appears to have taken her marital advice more seriously after they returned to the White House, as her public appearances reportedly dropped by 40 percent from what they were during the first Trump administration.

A Daily Beast analysis found that she appeared publicly on only 38 days during the first seven months of 2026, which amounts to roughly one appearance every six days, and in June and July, she was officially seen only five times.

Her last verified public appearance before a month-long absence that ended in August came on July 19, when she joined the president at the FIFA World Cup final.

She skipped major political events, including Senator Lindsey Graham's funeral ceremony, the dignified transfer of US soldiers killed in Iran, and the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner, all of which took place in July.

The First Reportedly Likes To Keep Her Distance : 'She Didn't Want To Be Around'

According to The Mirror US , former Trump White House official Sarah Matthews said Melania had a reputation for keeping her distance.

"That kind of sums it up, where it was this known thing that she was just not around and she didn't want to be around," she said.

Matthews noted Melania's preference for spending time in New York over the White House, which she reportedly viewed as "old and falling apart."

The Associated Press, however, revealed that the usually private first lady had a "burst of public activity" following the midterm elections that saw the Republicans lose control of Congress.

Melania Trump Says 'Communication Is the Most Important ' Thing In Her Marriage

Melania in her documentary clip also revealed what she believes is paramount for a healthy relationship. "I think in a relationship it's good to have communication; that's the most important," she said.

She explained that while speaking to one another is necessary, respecting a partner's belief and remaining firm in yours is also essential. "If you don't agree, OK, let's move on. It's normal!" Melania stated.

However, Trump biographer Michael Wolff has claimed that communication is exactly what is lacking in the relationship between the president and first lady of the United States.

Wolff claimed that the first couple "barely speak," and relationship expert Gemma Logan told the Irish Star that their rumored lack of this "most important" communication is indicative of an unhealthy marriage.

"A marriage where two people are reportedly barely speaking is clearly not in a healthy place. Communication is the heartbeat of any long-term relationship," the expert explained.

She noted that such couples who minimally communicate tend to live "parallel lives" instead of a shared one and that even when they spend time together they may not feel "emotionally connected" to each other.

Natalie Harp's Presence Also Explains The First Lady's Absence , According To Sources

Aside from simply believing time apart is healthy for her relationship, the frequent presence of White House aide and ardent Trump supporter Natalie Harp is rumored to contribute to the first lady's limited appearances beside Trump.

As reported by The Daily Beast , Wolff stated that Melania, who reportedly negotiates her appearances with Trump, "would not show up if Harp was around," and that "Since Harp was always around, Melania never was."

He further claimed that Harp superseded members of the White House staff and those of the president's family, including Melania. "Nobody got between Harp and Trump," the journalist added.

articles.title: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’: How Do Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson and Woody Harrelson appear
articles.summary: Warning: Spoilers ahead for the ending to “Sunrise on the Reaping.”
articles.body: Warning: Spoilers ahead for the ending to “Sunrise on the Reaping.” “Sunrise on the Reaping” is set more than 20 years before the events of the first “Hunger Games” film, but it still features an appearance from Katniss Everdeen — twice. Based on Suzanne Collins’ 2025 novel of the same name, “Sunrise on the Reaping,” which hit theaters Nov. 20, is the second “Hunger Games” prequel story. Where “Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes” told the origin story of President Snow, “Sunrise on the Reaping” follows Haymitch Abernathy. In 2012’s “The Hunger Games,” Haymitch, played by Woody Harrelson, is introduced as the oft-intoxicated, perpetually cynical District 12 Games victor serving as Katniss and Peeta’s mentor. He’s largely unlikable but honest, and steps up to support his tributes in the arena when he can. By the end of the trilogy with “Mockingjay,” it’s revealed Haymitch has deep-seated alliances with other victors of the Games, and he becomes one of the reluctant leaders of the revolt against the Capitol. Before “Sunrise on the Reaping,” fans only knew the basics of his story: He won the 50th Hunger Games, aka the Second Quarter, which had twice as many tributes. The novel and film, starring Joseph Zada as 16-year-old Haymitch, go deep into how that went down, from his unconventional reaping, how he become a rebel, the roots of his alcoholism and finally, why he lives all alone in Victor’s Village. But on the Oct. 28 episode of “Call Her Daddy,” Jennifer Lawrence confirmed she and Josh Hutcherson, who starred as Peeta, will appear in the new film. “Sunrise on the Reaping” is much darker compared to previous franchise installments. Essentially every person Haymitch loves or grows to love throughout the film is dead by the end. And even the people who haven’t been killed by Snow and the Capitol, Haymitch’s fear of making them a target leads him to push them away. This includes his friend from District 12 Burdock and his eventual wife, Asterid. When Haymitch returns after winning the Hunger Games, he’s iced out by most of the district due to the Capitol’s portrayal of Haymitch as ruthless, selfish and cowardly. But Burdock still tries to connect with his old friend, especially in the wake of the deaths of his family and girlfriend, Lenore Dove, in sudden tragedies. Haymitch turns to alcohol and withdraws from society, living in Victor’s Village. As time passes, he’s forced year after year to mentor the next set of tributes in the Games as District 12’s only winner. One of the final scenes sees Haymitch in the woods. He sees Burdock and Asterid out in nature with a newborn. He hides behind a tree as he watches the scene with the happy family. He locks eyes with the baby as she’s carried over her dad’s shoulder. He also overhears the parents coo their baby girl’s name: Katniss. Yes — Haymitch’s old friends are Burdock and Asterid Everdeen, Katniss Everdeen’s parents. That’s only the first time the character pops up. “Sunrise on the Reaping” has an epilogue, set well after the events of “Mockingjay” and the end of the annual Hunger Games. In the scene, Woody Harrelson reprises his role as Haymitch and stands in District 12 before a memorial dedicated to those killed by the Capitol. Lawrence’s Katniss and Hutcherson’s Peeta join him. They have a conversation reflecting on the end of the war and their newfound peace and wish Haymitch a happy birthday. It brings the film’s beginning, which reveals Haymitch’s birthday always fell on reaping day, full circle. The somber moment also shows that Haymitch was eventually able to make Lenore Dove’s wish — “don’t let the sun rise on the reaping” — come true, as Haymitch was part of the forces that ended the Hunger Games for good. Viewers later see Haymitch sitting in the field he used to meet Lenore Dove in. He’s surrounded by geese, an animal Lenore Dove used to raise. After Lawrence shared that she appears in “Sunrise on the Reaping,” she called her experience returning to the franchise “unbelievable.” “It was so crazy, because it was the same crew,” she said. “Josh and Woody — it was so emotional. Josh and I like, didn’t walk to the bathroom without our arms around each other.” “And Woody obviously came through the window of my hotel room uninvited,” she added with a grin. “It wouldn’t be the same if he listened to boundaries and used a door.” Lawrence, Hutcherson and Harrelson also attended the premiere of “Sunrise on the Reaping” in New York on Nov. 16 and appeared together in the cold open for “The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon” that same night.

articles.title: Macaulay Culkin returning for Home Alone sequel: report
articles.summary: Culkin last appeared in the franchise’s 1992 sequel ‘Home Alone 2: Lost in New York’
articles.body:
The 46-year-old is best-known for playing Kevin McCallister in the first two films in the franchise, 1990's original Home Alone and then the 1992 follow-up film Home Alone 2: Lost in New York. A third film was made in 1997 without him, and three more movies followed that.

Now, he will reportedly return for another sequel, according to Puck . The film is being produced by Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg and their Point Grey Pictures.

Puck reported that Rogen and Goldberg will work with Culkin on a script.

The Independent has contacted Disney for comment.

Rumors of a new Home Alone film began circulating earlier this year when Culkin signed with influential Hollywood talent agency CAA on the heels of a People report that Disney was working on a new installment in the film series.

A source told the publication at the time that the reboot came from Culkin's own idea, commenting: "It's in the early stages, very early. It's just an idea and an almost green light from Disney."

The source added: "Disney loved Macaulay's idea and everyone wants to see this happen."

In November last year, Culkin openly spoke about a potential sequel idea during his "A Nostalgic Night with Macaulay Culkin" tour.

During an appearance in Long Beach, the actor said: "I kind of had this idea, I'm either a widower or a divorcee. I'm raising a kid and all that stuff. I'm working really hard, and I'm not really paying enough attention, and the kid is kind of getting miffed at me, and then I get locked out."

Puck's new report comes just days after Culkin revisited his Home Alone character in an ad for McDonald's promoting a new meal named after the hit film franchise.

The Home Alone meal was announced Tuesday, just one day after the 36th anniversary of the film's release in theaters.

The ad pokes fun at Culkin's character Kevin McCallister, who was famously left behind when his family leaves for vacation.

In the fast food chain's ad, he stands in the middle of a deserted McDonald's location, shuttered due to a snowstorm, and laments: "Everyone disappeared, again."

He then dons a name tag introducing himself as "Kevin" before stepping into the role of a McDonald's employee, taking orders and preparing meals while simultaneously revealing the contents of the Home Alone meal.
